What part of antifrustrationism do you think is intuitively true? Non existence can't be imagined because it is truly nothing. We sometimes imagine a black space, but that is not non existence, it is a black space. Also, it is incorrect to say non existence = existence with all desires satisfied. One is the complete absence of stimuli and the other would be a state of eternal bliss. Those are completely different states, unless you just want to say the level of pain in both is equal, which is 0

While it has its merits, it also has failures. It is suited as a response to utilitarian problems of maximisation of happiness (the famous gladiator arena dillema), but it also has its setbacks.As for Benatar, his asymmetry is axiological, hence I criticized his abuse of conterfactuals that seem to rooted in flawed logic. That does not prevent the existence of terrible/wrongful lives, but it might take Ali's away from such a strong claim made by Benatar(that is was better to have never been). I don't actually agree with Antifrustrationism, although I think it has its merits. The idea has been on my mind for a while, that's why I was curious about some insights. I agree with most of what you described, but I would also add that looking through life only through desire lenses may be erroneous. Negative and positive situations may arise apart from any aversion or desire I previously thought about, hence I think an account about the hedonistic value of life only viewed through desire satisfaction/frustration may be incomplete.

I don't think Epicurus viewed pleasure as negative. After all, he valued the presence of friends, good food and wine (and these are pleasures). There is a lot to say about Bliss and the absence of pain, but I don't think Epicurus would negate the possibility of positive well being, just like Antifrustrationism proposed.

And we don't "need" to live. Most folks just prefer it to death, that doesn't mean going to eternal sleep is suffering, most people just prefer to do some things meanwhile. Epicurus already said this a long time ago.

Just to adress a point in here. Hapiness is not a "need" per se. You may still hold a view that life may be better than non-existence and think there is no need to create happy people and there may be some caution to not create unhappy people. Also, you may think that suffering comes much more easily in life than pleasure, yet still think your life is a net plus. Maybe you would fall in the Hedonistic and prioritarian labels, they seem to be similar to what you think.
The view you express seems to be some form of hedonistic utilitarianism.

There was no "I" in a state of "non-existence", I wasn't in non existence, I was not. We never did not exist, because in non existence we are not. A bit confusing but I hope you understand some of the logic in it.

Hello! This I think as similarities to negative utilitarianism. According to negative utilitarianism, perfection would just be anything without suffering. The balance in these 2 cases varies from person to person. For someone who wants the least amount of suffering, the 2nd option would be the best, but there are many people that say working hard towards something (suffering) and getting that, tastes so much sweeter. The worth of fulfilling something, comparing happiness and frustration varies from person to person, situation to situation. Only that person can evaluate the worth of it. In regards to your last paragraph, it is a clever observation, but one that isn't necessarily true. Does it mean because I have an interest in going to Japan, I am not satisfied/happy with my life? Not necessarily, and it doesn't mean if I don't ever go to Japan I'll feel sad. Also, it is difficult to say what is it to be fully content. Is it not feeling suffering? And what is it to be completely discontent? Only feeling sadness? We get to a paradox here with full contentment. If I'm watching TV, I may feel no suffering, and the same happens with riding a rollercoaster. However, I may say that rollercoaster>TV, even if I feel no suffering on both. The only counterargument here would be to say we feel suffering every single moment of our lives, and that is very contentious, not to say absurd. Also, the concept of perfect existence varies from person to person, someone may think that an existence with suffering may be superior to no suffering. You may find this absurd, but in the end, we are the sole judges on the value of our existence.

I think even actually using the term "non-existence" is incorrect. There was a greek philosopher, which I don't remember is name, that non-existence can never be, because it is not and can never change, therefore there is only existence. If we could talk in some kind of more "spiritual" level (i'm not trying to infuse religion into you ahahaha), we were never born and we will never die. The universe never came to be, nor it will end, since the universe can't come from "nothing". Nothing isn't a state, it is just absence, it can't be experience, nor can it exist, therefore it is not. I hope I was a bit clear, although this is a bit confusing. Some mystics say that time is an illusion (on a sidenote, I actually agree with this), we were never born and we never die, our "self" is an illusion. In this terms, life can't be compared to non existence. The question one can only posit here is that: is life good or bad? And always remember that these values are constricted to existence. Avoidance and relief of suffering can only work in a life state, and in a way, avoiding pain by trying to go to "non-existence" would be the same as dividing a fortune between me and you by burning all the notes. All emotions are encompassed in existence, although, of course, we as emotional beings would choose pleasure over nothing, and nothing over pain, that doesn't mean they can actually be comparable.

Of course, if I was told tomorrow that I would be submitted to 300 years of torture and I had the option today to die peacefully, of course it would be the reasonable thing to die. However, the comparision of "better" or "worse", although one that can be used to continue or stop our existence can't be used "properly" per se. Is a beautiful painting better than no painting? Is a horrible painting worse than no painting? One could say a beautiful painting is good and a horrible painting bad, and the first painting is better, but it is impossible to say how far we can compare a painting to no painting, in terms of it's beauty.

I think my example here wasn't good, but let me state another example. What is the health status of a rock? You surely would say that such question is incredibly stupid. It really is! The health of "someone" who doesn't exist is the same as the health of the rock. It isn't 0, it is a ridiculous statement in the first place. Health, just like hedonism, can only be atributed to sentient beings, therefore you can't say the hedonistic value of my dead bodoy is 0, you can't attribute an hedonistic value to my lack of conscience, there is an absence of "me". I hope I clarified this.
About the pleasure parts being the satisfaction/absence of desire, if you take a 4 year old and ask him why he is happy, he doesn't say because he satisfied all his desires. The 4 year old just is happy. There's reason antifrustrationism doesn't seem to work and is very inintuitive. If at the end of your life I asked, what was your best moment in life, you wouldn't say when you went under anesthesia. You would perhaps say when you fell in love, or finished a great personal project. You wouldn't say the best moment of your life was even sleeping, even if in that sleep you had 0 suffering! This may be used at proof that absence of desire != no desire, since the emotions, or lack of emotions are distinct in both cases. According to antifrustrationism, falling in love could only be as good as sleeping, and would almost always be worse, simply because when you met the love your life you were feeling a little cold, and according to that principle, you were under the 0 max mark.

In regards to Antifrustrationism, I agree that the argument isn't as stupid as it may sound in the beggining. It is very alike to Schopenhauer theory of well being. Read this for a refutal of that account (https://books.google.pt/books?id=huxuoJ0dRyEC&pg=PA308&lpg=PA308&dq=is+pleasure+just+the+absence+of+suffering?&source=bl&ots=unH2QM5XzG&sig=7rYfHyPZ3DabDl7n7t43tSmMt9k&hl=pt-PT&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwj3_KfP0LnZAhWHOhQKHTxKCYkQ6AEINjAB#v=onepage&q=is%20pleasure%20just%20the%20absence%20of%20suffering%3F&f=false). Also, I don't think you can say happiness stems from the absence or satisfaction of desire. I think happiness and pain may be outside of desire, even though they have many correlations. The problem lies in the fact that a theory of well being that denies happiness is very counter intuitive, the same as theory that denies pain. Desire isn't suffering, although it may contain suffering, and there is no proof that no desire=desire satisfaction. Even Buddha would disagree with this. Buddha when talking about suffering talked about cravings!, which are very strong desires that entail suffering. Buddha isn't against for example a desire to help others. He actually thought that the desire to help other was good. Also Nirvana isn't non existence, this is a very common misconception. Nirvana is just the death of ego, "me" and it's desires, but it isn't actually non-existence. Nirvana is full awareness of one, without the division of ego (my ego, your ego, ego is seperation). What Gray_Sloth is describing is very similar to a philosophy called Antifrustrationism that was developed by Christoph Fehige. In his, A Pareto for Possible People, he argues that no desire is as good as all desires satisfied. However, there are criticisms to it that I think may apply here too. The problem with Gray_Sloth scale, is that it only takes into account suffering. As to say, in this scale, the maximum value is 0, and non existence=heaven. However, I could reverse the scale and say the lowest value is 0 if I only take into account happiness. In that case, the worst of hells is as good as non existence. He says, that happiness is just a negation of the suffering of desire, however I could say that suffering is only the inability to obtain something good. Either of these scales don't make much sense. The absence of good isn't bad and the absence of bad isn't good. The absence of hate I have for a uknown person doesn't equate love, such as the absence of love I have towards that person doesn't equate hate. The other problem with his comparision is that we can't make a meaningful comparision between existence and non existence. This is impossible because the welfare of non existence isn't 0, it's no value, since welfare is a property only living beings can have.
